Q: Who defines the preconditions in Design by Contract? A:

The term 'precondition' is nebulous, and all pragmatic languages I know of check preconditions at all 3 feasible places:

  • Some preconditions are checked by the system, for example if you write in java void foo(String hello), one precondition of this method is that the first argument is either null or of type String, i.e. passing an Integer breaks a precondition. The compiler ( / class verifier) checks this precondition. You don't write if (!(x instanceof String)) nor should you.

  • Some preconditions are checked by the method itself, such as:

/// Does the foo thing.
///
/// @param v A non-negative integer.
public void foo(int v) {
  if (v < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("v is negative");
}
  • Some preconditions are not checked by the method itself; instead the specs spell out that the caller must guarantee it. Such as:
/// Creates a new TreeSet of type T.
///
/// @param type A type; its implementation of `Comparable` must follow the basic comparable rules. For example, if `a` is less than `b`, and `b` is less than `c`, then `a` must be considered less than `c`. Stupid things happen if you try to hand me a type that does not adhere to this precondition.

public void someOrderBasedSomething(Class<?> T) {
 ....
}

The halting problem says that it is in fact impossible for someOrderBasedSomething to actually check the precondition it has provided. It doesn't matter how much you'd love to thump some sort of style guide that demands that callers check all preconditions, but certain preconditions are uncheckable. Less dramatically, a bunch are in theory checkable but checking is pricey and onerous. Even if one is willing to pay that price, is one willing to pay it 50,000 times - every time the method is called? The sheer amount of damage done to the code base to introduce some sort of convoluted precondition checker caching system is vastly more significant than the very minor 'nit' of having a precondition that isn't actually verified.

At best we can introduce the notion that there's an order to these things:

  • The best 'precondition' is one expressed in the type system, such that the compiler/verifier checks it for you, and rather thoroughly at that.
  • The second best is one checked by the method, immediately.
  • The distant third best option is to throw in the towel, and in the name of pragmatism and/or choosing the lesser evil, puts the burden on the caller, and goes so far as to call out 'if you call me without checking, I make no guarantees or promises in any way about what's going to happen then'.

We can then conclude that any system that has to resort to option 3 is nominally 'worse' than one that doesn't. Which is fine - it means that if you can design a system to do the job without having to resort to the third option and without breaking other style and cleanliness rules, then, great, that one is 'better'. But rather often that is impossible: You can't write it without resorting to 'caller is responsible', or you can, but you break far more important rules in the process.

Q: fixing type error with concatenation and strings and lists A: 
city += m_cities

This is shorthand for

city = city + m_cities

In your case city is str and m_cities is list and python does not support action of + these. You might + only lists XOR only strs, therefore it would be valid to do

m_cities = m_cities + [city]

or in shorthand form

m_cities += [city]

thus

cities = ["New York", "Shanghai", "Munich", "Tokyo", "Dubai", "Mexico City", "São Paulo", "Hyderabad"]
m_cities = []
no_m_cities = []
for city in cities:
    if city.startswith('M'):
        m_cities += [city]
print(m_cities)

will output

['Munich', 'Mexico City']

Q: How can I insert multiple rows in SQLite? A:

You can't but I don't think you miss anything.

Because you call SQLite always in process, it almost doesn't matter in performance whether you execute 1 insert statement or 100 insert statements. The commit, however, takes a lot of time so put those 100 inserts inside a transaction.

SQLite is much faster when you use parameterized queries (far less parsing needed) so I wouldn't concatenate big statements like this:

insert into mytable (col1, col2)
select 'a','b'
union
select 'c','d'
union ...

They need to be parsed again and again because every concatenated statement is different.

Q: tmux + micro text editor: shift-arrow echo keycode A:

सेवा में,

थाना प्रभारी महोदय,

(थाने का नाम), (शहर का नाम)

विषय: मारपीट और गाली-गलौज की शिकायत

महोदय,

मैं (आपका नाम), निवासी (पूरा पता), मेहनत-मजदूरी करता हूँ। मैं यह लिखित शिकायत प्रस्तुत कर रहा हूँ कि दिनांक 28/03/2026 को दोपहर लगभग 02:00 बजे मैं घर से बाजार जाने के लिए निकला था।

जैसे ही मैं (पेसटरी का नाम/स्थान) के पास पुलिया पर पहुँचा, तभी (आरोपी 1: मु़ेमनीप िहरवार), (आरोपी 2: आकाश उफ टछूु), (आरोपी 3: यश िहरवार) ने मुझे रोक लिया और गाली-गलौज करते हुए मारपीट की। मुझे गाल और पीठ पर चोटें आईं।

तभी मेरे भाई (संजू) और पड़ोसी (मोहान अहिरवार, पिता का नाम: __; सौरभ कशवाह, पिता का नाम: __; संजू, पिता का नाम: _________) मौके पर आए और **उन्होंने आरोपियों से मारपीट की**।

अतः आपसे निवेदन है कि उपरोक्त आरोपियों के खिलाफ भारतीय दंड संहिता (IPC) की धारा 323 (मारपीट), 294 (गाली-गलौज) और 341 (रास्ता रोकना) के तहत मामला दर्ज कर उचित कानूनी कार्रवाई करने की कृपा करें।

धन्यवाद।

भवदीय,

नाम: __________

भाई का नाम: संजू

पड़ोसी का नाम:

- मोहन अहिरवार, पिता का नाम: _________

- सौरभ कशवाह, पिता का नाम: _________

- संजू, पिता का नाम: _________

मोबाइल नंबर: __________

पता: __________

हस्ताक्षर: __________

तारीख: 28/03/2026
